title: The posterior predictive
objectives: Predict new data from the posterior and check a model against it.

screens.title: The next ten orders
screens.prose: After 40 orders the fill rate is Beta(15, 35). The desk sends 10 more orders tomorrow. One guess plugs a single rate into a Binomial(10, $p$). The dashed lines are the answer that keeps the doubt about $p$. Move $p$ and compare the tails.

derive.caption: Plug-in Binomial(10, {{fixed(p, 2)}}): $P(X \ge 5)$ = {{fixed(values['5'] + values['6'] + values['7'] + values['8'] + values['9'] + values['10'], 4)}}. Predictive (dashed): 0.1702.

screens.question: At $p = 0.3$, what is the plug-in chance of 5 or more fills?

hints.text: The caption adds the bars from 5 to 10.
Set the slider to 0.30.
About 0.150.

feedback.correct: 0.1503, below the predictive's 0.1702: no single $p$ carries the doubt about $p$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $p = 0.3$ and read the caption.

byKey.pred: That is the predictive's tail, the dashed lines. The question asks for the plug-in bars.

explain.text: Binomial(10, 0.3) gives $P(X \ge 5) = 0.1503$. The predictive gives 0.1702, because high values of $p$ stay possible.

screens.title: Averaging over the posterior
screens.prose: The **posterior predictive** averages the data model over the posterior: $P(X = j) = \int \binom{10}{j}p^j(1 - p)^{10 - j}\,\pi(p \mid \text{data})\,dp$. For a Beta posterior this is the beta-binomial. Both have mean 3. The beta-binomial's variance is $10 \times 0.3 \times 0.7 \times (1 + 9/51)$.
screens.question: What is the predictive variance of tomorrow's fills?

hints.text: Start from the binomial variance $10 \times 0.3 \times 0.7$.
Multiply 2.1 by $1 + 9/51$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the binomial variance by $1 + 9/51$.

byKey.plug: That is the plug-in binomial's variance. It ignores the doubt about $p$.
byKey.sd: That is the standard deviation. The question asks for the variance.

explain.text: The predictive carries two kinds of uncertainty: the binomial's noise and the doubt about $p$. Its variance is 2.4706 against the plug-in's 2.1.

screens.prose: `scipy.stats.betabinom(10, 15, 35).pmf` and the formula $\binom{10}{j}B(j + 15, 45 - j)/B(15, 35)$ give the same pmf.
screens.question: What is the predictive chance of 5 or more fills?

hints.text: Add the predictive column from $j = 5$ down.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the predictive rows $j = 5$ to 10.

byKey.four: You started at $j = 4$. Five or more starts at 5.

screens.title: Next year's defaults
screens.prose: The default posterior Gamma(17, rate 6) makes next year's count negative binomial with $r = 17$, $p = 6/7$. Its mean is 2.8333 and its variance is the mean times $1 + 1/6$.
screens.question: What is the predictive variance of next year's defaults?

hints.text: A Poisson's variance equals its mean; the doubt about $\lambda$ adds to it.

feedback.correct: 3.3056, against 2.8333 for a Poisson with the mean plugged in.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the mean by $1 + 1/6$.

byKey.pois: That is the plug-in Poisson's variance, equal to its mean.
byKey.sixth: You divided by $1 + 1/6$. The doubt about $\lambda$ widens the spread.

explain.text: $\text{Var} = E[\lambda] + \text{Var}(\lambda) = 2.8333 + 17/36 = 3.3056$. Then $P(\ge 6) = 0.0829$ against the plug-in Poisson's 0.0681.

screens.title: The capital model
screens.prose: A credit desk holds extra capital if six or more defaults next year have an 8% chance or more. The analyst plugs the posterior mean 2.8333 into a Poisson: $P(\ge 6) = 0.0681$. The predictive gives 0.0829.
screens.question: What should the desk do?

options.text: Hold the capital: the predictive 0.0829 is above 8%
Skip it: the plug-in 0.0681 is below 8%
options.why: The plug-in treats $\lambda$ as known. It understates the spread, so its tail is too thin.

options.text: Average the two, 0.0755, and skip it
options.why: Averaging a right and a wrong figure gives a wrong one.

hints.text: Which figure carries the doubt about $\lambda$?
The plug-in uses one $\lambda$ as if it were known.
The predictive's tail is the honest one.

feedback.correct: The predictive's 0.0829 crosses the 8% line, so the desk holds capital.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Plugging in the mean removes the doubt about $\lambda$.

byKey.plug: You trusted the plug-in. Its tail, 0.0681, is too small because $\lambda$ is not known.

explain.text: Plugging in a posterior mean drops the doubt about the parameter. Tails come out too thin: 0.0681 against 0.0829 here, and 0.1503 against 0.1702 for fills.

screens.title: Checking the model on D3
screens.prose: Fit a Poisson to D3, lesson 3's 200 days of fill counts, with a weak Gamma(1, rate 0.1) prior. D3 sums to 881, so the posterior is Gamma(882, rate 200.1). Draw $\lambda$, then 200 Poisson days, 200,000 times. Count zero days in each replicate.

params.xLabel: Zero days in a replicated 200-day set

screens.question: On average, how many zero days does a replicated data set have?

hints.text: Each day is zero with chance $e^{-\lambda}$.
Average $200e^{-\lambda}$ over Gamma(882, rate 200.1).

feedback.correct: About 2.46, while D3 has 28: the model fails the check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average $200e^{-\lambda}$ over the posterior.

byKey.obs: That is D3's own count. The question asks what the model predicts.
byKey.plug: That is $200e^{-4.4078} = 2.436$, the mean plugged in. Averaging over $\lambda$ gives 2.46.

explain.text: Replicates average 2.46 zero days and the largest of 200,000 is 13. D3 has 28, so the posterior predictive $p$ sits at its floor, $1/200{,}001$. The variance check fails the same way.

screens.title: A check that cannot fail
screens.prose: Pick the check statistic before looking at the data. Some statistics are fitted by the model itself. The Poisson posterior's mean, 4.4078, sits on D3's mean, 4.405.

params.xLabel: Zero days in a replicated 200-day set

screens.question: Which statistic would this Poisson model pass on almost any data set?

options.why: The model fails it on D3: 28 against about 2.46.
The model fails it: D3's variance is 17.1 against about 4.4.
D3's 23 is far in the tail of a Poisson with mean 4.4.

hints.text: Which number did the fit match to the data?
The posterior mean of $\lambda$ is close to the sample mean.
The mean.

feedback.correct: The fit matches the mean by construction, so that check proves nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which statistic does the model fit by construction?

byKey.zero: That is the check D3 fails. A good check targets what the model might get wrong.

explain.text: The posterior mean of $\lambda$ tracks the sample mean, so replicated means match D3's. Zero days and the variance are what a Poisson cannot fit here.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose:
Predict by averaging the data model over the posterior:
$$p(\tilde y \mid y) = \int p(\tilde y \mid \theta)\,\pi(\theta \mid y)\,d\theta$$
Check a model by comparing a statistic $T$ of the data with $T$ on replicates from this predictive: $p = P(T(\tilde y) \ge T(y) \mid y)$.
screens.question: Why is the predictive wider than the plug-in?

options.text: It adds the doubt about $\theta$ to the noise of the data model

options.why: The prior enters once, through the posterior.
Both use all the data. Only one keeps the doubt about $\theta$.

feedback.correct: Two kinds of uncertainty add up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does plugging in throw away?

byKey.prior: You thought the prior was counted twice. It enters once, through the posterior.

screens.title: Predictive and check in code
screens.prose: Write the beta-binomial pmf with `betaln`, its upper tail, and a posterior predictive check for a Gamma-Poisson model. Draw all $\lambda$ values first, then the replicates.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

def ppc_pvalue(y, stat, a0, b0, n_rep, seed):
    """Posterior predictive p, (1 + #{T(rep) >= T(y)}) / (n_rep + 1),

screens.title: Quiet days
screens.prose: A researcher prices a strategy that earns only on days with no fills: quiet markets. The pricing uses the Poisson model of D3, which puts about 2.46 zero days in 200. D3 itself had 28.

params.xLabel: Zero days in a replicated 200-day set

screens.question: What should the researcher conclude?

options.text: The model fails a check on exactly what the strategy trades on, so do not price with it
The posterior mean matches the data, so the model is fine
options.why: The mean is fitted by construction. Zero days are what the strategy needs, and the model gets them wrong.

options.text: Run more replicates until one reaches 28
options.why: Over 200,000 replicates the largest was 13. More runs only confirm the failure.

hints.text: Which feature of the data does the strategy use?
The model predicts about 2.46 quiet days; there were 28.
A failed check on the traded feature rules the model out.

feedback.correct: Check the model on the feature you trade; here it fails.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The strategy lives on zero days.

byKey.fine: You trusted the mean check, which any Poisson passes. Zero days are what matter here.

explain.text: The predictive puts 2.46 zero days in 200, against 28 seen. Pricing quiet days with this model would understate them by a factor of about 11.

ideas: The posterior predictive averages the data model over the posterior: beta-binomial for fills, negative binomial for defaults.
Plugging in the posterior mean understates the spread: 0.1503 against 0.1702, and 0.0681 against 0.0829.
A predictive check compares a chosen statistic with replicates: D3's 28 zero days against about 2.46 rejects the Poisson.

formula.name: Posterior predictive
formula.tex: p(\tilde y \mid y) = \int p(\tilde y \mid \theta)\,\pi(\theta \mid y)\,d\theta
formula.note: Its variance is the model's noise plus the doubt about $\theta$.

quiz.prose: An analyst looks at the data, sees an odd feature, then checks the model on exactly that feature. It fails.
quiz.question: What is wrong with the procedure?

options.text: The statistic was chosen after looking, so the $p$ overstates the evidence
Nothing: a failed check is always decisive
options.why: Any data set has some odd feature. Hunting for it makes a failure likely by chance.

options.text: They should have checked the mean
options.why: The mean is fitted by construction, so that check proves nothing.

feedback.correct: Choose the statistic from the use of the model, before looking.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. When was the statistic chosen?

byKey.never: You treated the check as decisive. A statistic chosen by looking will often fail by chance.

explain.text: A check picked after looking is a search over many features. Pick the statistic from what the model will be used for, as with zero days.
